Introduction

Author's Preface & Epigraph

📖 pp. 4–9 (Vintage Original PDF) 2 Paragraphs 313 Words Est. ~1 min 🎯 Target: 15–20 min
Original 1955 Translation Page 4 • §1 of 2

FOR ME “The Myth of Sisyphus” marks the beginning of an idea which I was to pursue in The Rebel. It attempts to resolve the problem of suicide, as The Rebel attempts to resolve that of murder, in both cases without the aid of eternal values which, temporarily perhaps, are absent or distorted in contemporary Europe. The fundamental subject of “The Myth of Sisyphus” is this: it is legitimate and necessary to wonder whether life has a meaning; therefore it is legitimate to meet the problem of suicide face to face. The answer, underlying and appearing through the paradoxes which cover it, is this: even if one does not believe in God, suicide is not legitimate. Written fifteen years ago, in 1940, amid the French and European disaster, this book declares that even within the limits of nihilism it is possible to find the means to proceed beyond nihilism. In all the books I have written since, I have attempted to pursue this direction. Although “The Myth of Sisyphus” poses mortal problems, it sums itself up for me as a lucid invitation to live and to create, in the very midst of the desert.

Dignified Modern Translation Page 4•§1 of 2 (50%)
187w • ~47s

For me, The Myth of Sisyphus marks the birth of a central intuition that I would later develop in The Rebel. It seeks to resolve the question of suicide, just as The Rebel seeks to resolve the question of murder—in both instances without relying on transcendent, eternal values, which for now are absent or broken in modern Europe. The foundational premise of this book is straightforward: it is entirely legitimate and necessary to ask whether life possesses meaning; therefore, one must confront the reality of suicide directly. The definitive conclusion, emerging through all the paradoxes that frame it, is this: even in the absence of God, suicide is not a valid answer. Written fifteen years ago in 1940, during the catastrophe of the war in France and Europe, this work affirms that even within the depths of nihilism, one can discover the strength to transcend nihilism. In all the books I have written since, I have attempted to pursue this direction. Although this essay wrestles with deadly questions, for me it stands as an uncompromising invitation to live and to create—directly in the heart of the wasteland.

The Philosophical Move

Camus summarizes his entire thesis before the book begins: This is an anti-nihilist work. Recognizing that life has no cosmic purpose does not justify self-destruction; it makes creative living even more urgent and heroic.

Original 1955 Translation Page 9 • §2 of 2

THE PAGES that follow deal with an absurd sensitivity that can be found widespread in the age—and not with an absurd philosophy which our time, properly speaking, has not known. It is therefore simply fair to point out, at the outset, what these pages owe to certain contemporary thinkers. It is so far from my intention to hide this that they will be found cited and commented upon throughout this work. But it is useful to note at the same time that the absurd, hitherto taken as a conclusion, is considered in this essay as a starting-point. In this sense it may be said that there is something provisional in my commentary: one cannot prejudge the position it entails. There will be found here merely the description, in the pure state, of an intellectual malady. No metaphysic, no belief is involved in it for the moment. These are the limits and the only bias of this book.

Dignified Modern Translation Page 9•§2 of 2 (100%)
126w • ~32s

The pages that follow describe a widespread contemporary sensitivity to the absurd—not an established 'absurd philosophy,' which our era has not actually developed. It is only honest to acknowledge from the beginning how much this inquiry owes to contemporary philosophers; far from concealing these influences, they will be openly analyzed throughout this text. Crucially, however, while previous thinkers treated the Absurd as a final dead-end conclusion, in this book the Absurd is treated purely as a starting point. My analysis is therefore provisional: one should not assume the final verdict beforehand. What you will find here is simply the unvarnished diagnosis of an intellectual condition. No metaphysical system, no theology, and no dogma are assumed. That is the exact scope and sole boundary of this book.

The Philosophical Move

The Pindar epigraph provides the moral motto of the book: reject dreams of immortality (heaven) and milk mortal life for maximum intensity. Camus also clarifies: Absurdity is not his conclusion—it is merely his starting point.

Part I: An Absurd Reasoning

1. Absurdity and Suicide

📖 pp. 10–14 (Vintage Original PDF) 8 Paragraphs 986 Words Est. ~4 min 🎯 Target: 15–20 min
Original 1955 Translation Page 10 • §1 of 8

There is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide. Judging whether life is or is not worth living amounts to answering the fundamental question of philosophy. All the rest—whether or not the world has three dimensions, whether the mind has nine or twelve categories—comes afterwards. These are games; one must first answer. And if it is true, as Nietzsche claims, that a philosopher, to deserve our respect, must preach by example, you can appreciate the importance of that reply, for it will precede the definitive act. These are facts the heart can feel; yet they call for careful study before they become clear to the intellect.

There is only one genuinely serious philosophical question, and that is suicide. Deciding whether life is or is not worth living is the fundamental question of philosophy. Everything else—whether the physical universe has three dimensions, or whether human cognition operates through nine or twelve categories—is secondary. Those are intellectual pastimes; one must answer this first. And if Nietzsche is correct that a philosopher only commands our respect if they teach by personal example, one can appreciate the gravity of the answer, for it directly precedes an irreversible act. These are realities the heart senses instinctively, yet they demand rigorous examination before they become clear to the intellect.

The Philosophical Move

Camus establishes a strict hierarchy of urgency: metaphysical and epistemological theories are intellectual games; the question of survival and value precedes all contemplation.

Original 1955 Translation Page 10 • §2 of 8

If I ask myself how to judge that this question is more urgent than that, I reply that one judges by the actions it entails. I have never seen anyone die for the ontological argument. Galileo, who held a scientific truth of great importance, abjured it with the greatest ease as soon as it endangered his life. In a certain sense, he did right. That truth was not worth the stake. Whether the earth or the sun revolves around the other is a matter of profound indifference. To tell the truth, it is a futile question. On the other hand, I see many people die because they judge that life is not worth living. I see others paradoxically getting killed for the ideas or illusions that give them a reason for living (what is called a reason for living is also an excellent reason for dying). I therefore conclude that the meaning of life is the most urgent of questions.

Dignified Modern Translation Page 10•§2 of 8 (25%)
158w • ~40s

How does one determine whether one question is more urgent than another? By the actions it demands. No one has ever died defending an abstract proof for the existence of God. When Galileo discovered a scientific truth of immense importance, he renounced it without hesitation the moment his life was threatened—and in a sense, he was right. That truth was not worth burning at the stake for. Whether the Earth orbits the Sun or the Sun orbits the Earth is a matter of profound indifference to our day-to-day existence; in truth, it is an idle question. In contrast, I see men choose death because they conclude life is not worth living. Paradoxically, I see others die for the very ideals or illusions that give them a reason to live (for what provides a reason for living also provides a compelling reason for dying). I conclude, therefore, that the meaning of life is the most urgent question of all.

The Philosophical Move

Existential truth vs. theoretical truth. Galileo rightly refused martyrdom for astronomical physics because scientific facts do not alter the lived weight of existence, whereas meaning dictates literal life and death.

Solely the balance between evidence and lyricism can allow us to achieve simultaneously emotion and lucidity. In a subject at once so humble and so heavy with emotion, the learned and classical dialectic must yield, one can see, to a more modest attitude of mind deriving at one and the same time from common sense and understanding.

The Philosophical Move

Camus defines his methodology: balancing empirical fact (La Palice) with emotional passion (Don Quixote), discarding scholastic jargon in favor of clear psychological awareness.

Suicide has never been dealt with except as a social phenomenon. On the contrary, we are concerned here, at the outset, with the relationship between individual thought and suicide. An act like this is prepared within the silence of the heart, as is a great work of art. The man himself is ignorant of it. One evening he pulls the trigger or jumps. Of an apartment-building manager who had killed himself I was told that he had lost his daughter five years before, that he had changed greatly since, and that that experience had “undermined” him. A more exact word cannot be imagined. Beginning to think is beginning to be undermined. Society has but little connection with such beginnings. The worm is in man’s heart. That is where it must be sought. One must follow and understand this fatal game that leads from lucidity in the face of existence to flight from light.

Suicide has almost always been treated merely as a sociological statistic. Here, by contrast, we are concerned from the start with the intimate connection between private consciousness and self-destruction. Such an act matures in the silence of the heart, much like a great work of art. The individual himself is often unaware of its silent gestation until, one evening, he pulls the trigger or leaps. Of a building manager who took his own life, I was told he had lost his daughter five years earlier, had altered profoundly thereafter, and that the ordeal had 'undermined' him from within. A more precise term cannot be conceived. To begin to think is to begin to be undermined. Society has little bearing on these internal origins. The parasite resides within the human heart; that is where it must be sought. We must trace this fatal progression from the first lucid confrontation with existence to the eventual flight from reality.

The Philosophical Move

Camus shifts suicide from social statistics to private internal decay. 'To begin to think is to begin to be undermined' marks the terrifying rupture when conscious reflection destroys habitual numbness.

The Philosophical Move

Defining suicide as the breaking of habit. We persist in life through mechanical momentum; voluntary death is the sudden realization that the momentum has no justification.

The primary form of evasion—the fatal trap that forms the third major theme of this essay—is hope: whether the religious hope for an afterlife that must be earned, or the secular deception of living not for existence itself, but for some grand future ideology that claims to transcend and elevate life, yet ultimately betrays it.

The Philosophical Move

Exposing our dual survival buffers: (1) the biological body's ancient instinct to survive, and (2) the intellectual escape hatch of 'Hope' (postponing reality for heaven or a utopian future).

2. Absurd Walls

It happens that the stage sets collapse. Rising, streetcar, four hours in the office or the factory, meal, streetcar, four hours of work, meal, sleep, and Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday and Saturday according to the same rhythm—this path is easily followed most of the time. But one day the “why” arises and everything begins in that weariness tinged with amazement. “Begins”—this is important. Weariness comes at the end of the acts of a mechanical life, but at the same time it inaugurates the impulse of consciousness. It awakens consciousness and provokes what follows. What follows is the gradual return into the chain or it is the definitive awakening.

Yet there are times when the theatrical scenery collapses. Waking, the streetcar, four hours in the office or factory, a meal, the streetcar, four hours of labor, a meal, sleep, and Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday unfolding to the identical rhythm—this routine is followed effortlessly for years. Yet one day, the question 'Why?' arises, and everything begins in a state of weariness mingled with astonishment. 'Begins'—this distinction is vital. Exhaustion concludes a life of mechanical habit, yet it simultaneously inaugurates the birth of genuine consciousness. Camus charts the sudden collapse of daily autopilot. The routine protects us from awareness; the intrusion of 'Why?' ends unconscious existence and forces a choice between conscious lucidity or relapse into stupor.

The betrayal of time. We live on credit projected into the future, forgetting that the destination is death. Turning thirty marks the threshold where time ceases to be an ally and reveals itself as an executioner.

3. Philosophical Suicide

The feeling of the absurd is not, for all that, the notion of the absurd. It lays the foundations for it, and that is all. It is not limited to that notion, except in the brief moment when it passes judgment on the universe. Subsequently it has a chance of going further. It is alive; in other words, it must die or else reverberate. So it is with the themes we have gathered together. But there again what interests me is not works or minds, criticism of which would call for another form and another place, but the discovery of what their conclusions have in common. Never, perhaps, have minds been so different. And yet we recognize as identical the spiritual landscapes in which they get under way. Likewise, despite such dissimilar zones of knowledge, the cry that terminates their itinerary rings out in the same way. It is evident that the thinkers we have just recalled have a common climate. To say that that climate is deadly scarcely amounts to playing on words. Living under that stifling sky forces one to get away or to stay. The important thing is to find out how people get away in the first case and why people stay in the second case. This is how I define the problem of suicide and the possible interest in the conclusions of existential philosophy.

The visceral feeling of the absurd is not yet the philosophical concept of the absurd. It provides the initial foundation, nothing more. Nor is the feeling confined to that concept, except in the brief flash when consciousness passes judgment on the universe. From that initial spark, it has the potential to evolve. It is a living impulse; it must either wither away or echo through one's entire existence. The same is true of the philosophical themes we have assembled. Yet my concern is not with critiquing specific authors or intellectual systems—which would demand a different forum—but with uncovering what their final conclusions share. Perhaps thinkers have never been so radically different from one another. And yet we recognize the identical spiritual terrain from which they all set out. In the same way, despite exploring entirely different fields of knowledge, the final cry that concludes their intellectual journeys sounds the exact same note. It is clear that these thinkers inhabit a single shared atmosphere. To call that atmosphere lethal is no mere figure of speech. Living under that suffocating sky forces a stark choice: flee or remain. The essential task is to discover how people escape in the first case, and why people choose to stay in the second. This is how I frame the question of suicide and our legitimate interest in the conclusions of existential philosophy.

The Philosophical Move

Camus distinguishes the raw visceral experience of absurdity from its rigorous conceptualization. Existential thinkers from wildly divergent backgrounds all encounter the same lethal, suffocating realization; Camus's diagnostic goal is to determine who flees through escapism and who possesses the fortitude to remain.

Original 1955 Translation Page 29 • §3 of 28

If I accuse an innocent man of a monstrous crime, if I tell a virtuous man that he has coveted his own sister, he will reply that this is absurd. His indignation has its comical aspect. But it also has its fundamental reason. The virtuous man illustrates by that reply the definitive antinomy existing between the deed I am attributing to him and his lifelong principles. “It’s absurd” means “It’s impossible” but also “It’s contradictory.” If I see a man armed only with a sword attack a group of machine guns, I shall consider his act to be absurd. But it is so solely by virtue of the disproportion between his intention and the reality he will encounter, of the contradiction I notice between his true strength and the aim he has in view. Likewise we shall deem a verdict absurd when we contrast it with the verdict the facts apparently dictated. And, similarly, a demonstration by the absurd is achieved by comparing the consequences of such a reasoning with the logical reality one wants to set up. In all these cases, from the simplest to the most complex, the magnitude of the absurdity will be in direct ratio to the distance between the two terms of my comparison. There are absurd marriages, challenges, rancors, silences, wars, and even peace treaties. For each of them the absurdity springs from a comparison. I am thus justified in saying that the feeling of absurdity does not spring from the mere scrutiny of a fact or an impression, but that it bursts from the comparison between a bare fact and a certain reality, between an action and the world that transcends it. The absurd is essentially a divorce. It lies in neither of the elements compared; it is born of their confrontation.

If I accuse an innocent person of a monstrous atrocity, or tell an honorable man that he has lusted after his own sister, he will protest that the accusation is absurd. His moral indignation may seem almost comical. Yet his outrage rests on solid philosophical ground. By that reply, the honorable man highlights the irreconcilable contradiction between the crime attributed to him and the lifelong principles by which he lives. In common speech, 'That is absurd' means both 'That is impossible' and 'That is self-contradictory.' If I witness a soldier armed only with a sword charging a battery of machine guns, I judge his action to be absurd. Yet his act is absurd only because of the vast disproportion between his intention and the physical reality awaiting him—the glaring contradiction between his actual strength and the objective he pursues. In the same way, we call a judicial verdict absurd when we weigh it against the verdict demanded by the facts. Similarly, a mathematical proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum) operates by comparing the logical consequences of a premise with the reality one intends to establish. In every instance, from the mundane to the complex, the magnitude of absurdity corresponds directly to the gulf separating the two elements of the comparison. There are absurd marriages, absurd vendettas, absurd silences, absurd wars, and even absurd peace treaties. In each case, absurdity arises exclusively from a comparison. I am therefore justified in asserting that the feeling of the absurd never arises from examining an isolated fact or emotion in a vacuum; it erupts from the collision between a raw fact and a surrounding reality, between a human action and the larger context that envelops it. The Absurd is fundamentally a divorce. It resides in neither element alone; it is born entirely of their collision.

The Philosophical Move

The foundational definition of the Relational Absurd. Absurdity is never an inherent quality of an object, a person, or the universe in isolation; it is strictly a mathematical ratio—the friction generated by comparing human intent with recalcitrant reality.

Mystical traditions have long made us familiar with such dialectical acrobatics. As a subjective posture, they are as psychologically defensible as any other. But for now, I proceed on the assumption that our central problem must be addressed with unflinching seriousness. Without passing prior judgment on the moral or spiritual worth of mysticism, my sole task is to see whether it satisfies the rules of my inquiry—whether it respects the integrity of the conflict before us. This brings me directly to Leon Chestov. A commentator records a striking remark of his: 'The only true solution,' Chestov observed, 'is found precisely where human reason sees no solution whatever. For if reason could solve it, why would we need God? We turn to God only to obtain the impossible. For what is merely possible, humanity suffices on its own.' If there is a coherent Chestovian philosophy, it is entirely distilled in those sentences. For when, at the climax of his ferocious critiques, Chestov uncovers the irremediable absurdity of all existence, he does not conclude: 'This is the Absurd,' but rather: 'This is God; we must cast ourselves upon Him, even if He defies every category of rational thought.' To prevent any misunderstanding, the Russian thinker even suggests that this God may be vengeful, terrifying, incomprehensible, and contradictory; yet the more grotesque His visage appears, the more absolute His power becomes. His grandeur is His very incoherence. His inhumanity is the ultimate proof of His existence. One must plunge blindly into His embrace, using this leap of faith to shatter the illusions of human reason. For Chestov, therefore, recognizing the absurd is synonymous with surrendering to it. To become conscious of absurdity is already to embrace it, and the entire momentum of his thought is designed to expose the Absurd only so that an immense, miraculous hope may erupt from its ashes. I repeat: such an attitude is humanly understandable. But my commitment here is to pursue a single, rigorous question to its ultimate conclusion. I am not evaluating the psychological warmth of religious faith or mystical rapture. A person has an entire lifetime for that. I realize that the academic rationalist finds Chestov's anti-rational stance exasperating. Yet I agree with Chestov against the complacent rationalist—and my only concern is whether he remains faithful to the iron demands of the Absurd.

The intoxicating appeal of the irrational and the hunger for religious rapture lure the lucid intellect away from the reality of the Absurd. Everything is sacrificed here to the irrational, and, the demand for clarity being conjured away, the absurd disappears with one of the terms of its comparison. The absurd man, on the other hand, does not undertake such a leveling process. He recognizes the struggle, does not absolutely scorn reason, and admits the irrational. Thus he again embraces in a single glance all the data of experience and he is little inclined to leap before knowing. This leap of faith clarifies the genuine anatomy of the Absurd. We already know that the Absurd possesses no validity outside an exact equilibrium—that it resides strictly in the relation between two poles, never in either pole isolated on its own. Yet Chestov loads all the weight onto a single term, shattering the scale. Our hunger for meaning and our yearning for the absolute are intelligible only because human reason can, in fact, explain many practical aspects of our world. It is pointless to reject human reason entirely. Reason has its legitimate domain where it remains genuinely effective. That domain is the realm of direct human experience. Because reason succeeds locally, we demand that it explain the cosmos as a whole. When it fails to do so—and when the Absurd is born—it emerges at the exact frontier where effective yet bounded reason collides with the encroaching irrational. When Chestov attacks the Hegelian doctrine that 'the solar system moves in accordance with immutable laws, and those laws constitute its reason,' or when he battles Spinoza's totalizing rationalism, he concludes that all human reason is utterly futile. From that conclusion, by an effortless but illegitimate reversal, he proclaims the supreme sovereignty of the irrational. Yet that deduction is completely invalid. Here we must introduce the concepts of boundaries and operational levels. The physical laws of nature may function reliably up to a specific threshold, beyond which they break down and generate absurdity. Alternatively, natural laws may be entirely valid at the level of empirical description without offering ultimate metaphysical explanation. Chestov sacrifices everything to the irrational; by banishing the human demand for clarity, he dissolves the Absurd by deleting one half of the equation. The lucid absurd thinker refuses this false leveling. He sustains the combat: he neither scorns practical reason nor denies cosmic silence. He takes in the full spectrum of reality with an unwavering gaze, refusing to leap into the dark before he understands where he lands. He recognizes, simply and unblinkingly, that within this heightened state of awareness, there is no longer any room for hope.

The Philosophical Move

Refuting the false dichotomy: Rationalism vs. Irrationalism. Reason is effective within human experience, but silent on cosmic meaning. Chestov illegitimately infers that because reason cannot explain everything, it is useless and the irrational is God. Camus insists on maintaining the balance without leaping.

Between the irrational of the world and the insurgent nostalgia of the absurd, he does not maintain the equilibrium. He does not respect the relationship that constitutes, properly speaking, the feeling of absurdity. Sure of being unable to escape the irrational, he wants at least to save himself from that desperate nostalgia that seems to him sterile and devoid of implication. But if he may be right on this point in his judgment, he could not be in his negation. If he substitutes for his cry of revolt a frantic adherence, at once he is led to blind himself to the absurd which hitherto enlightened him and to deify the only certainty he henceforth possesses, the irrational. The important thing, as Abbé Galiani said to Mme d’Epinay, is not to be cured, but to live with one’s ailments. Kierkegaard wants to be cured. To be cured is his frenzied wish, and it runs throughout his whole journal. The entire effort of his intelligence is to escape the antinomy of the human condition. An all the more desperate effort since he intermittently perceives its vanity when he speaks of himself, as if neither fear of God nor piety were capable of bringing him to peace. Thus it is that, through a strained subterfuge, he gives the irrational the appearance and God the attributes of the absurd: unjust, incoherent, and incomprehensible. Intelligence alone in him strives to stifle the underlying demands of the human heart. Since nothing is proved, everything can be proved.

I am not concerned here with the passionate theology to which this stance gives voice. My sole task is to determine whether the reality of the Absurd and its internal logic justify such a retreat. On that count, the answer is an unequivocal no. Re-examining the structure of the Absurd reveals the underlying mechanism of Kierkegaard's strategy. He fails to maintain the equilibrium between cosmic silence and the human hunger for clarity. He violates the relational tension that alone constitutes the reality of absurdity. Certain that he cannot escape the irrational universe, he seeks at least to purge himself of that agonizing hunger for reason, which strikes him as barren and hopeless. But even if his psychological assessment of that torment is understandable, his philosophical renunciation is completely illegitimate. By replacing his cry of defiance with a desperate act of religious devotion, he immediately blinds himself to the lucidity that previously guided him, deifying the irrational as his only remaining anchor. As the Abbé Galiani once remarked to Madame d'Épinay, the essential task is not to be cured, but to learn how to live with one's affliction. Yet Kierkegaard is desperate to be cured. To be healed of the human condition is his manic, all-consuming obsession, pulsing through every page of his private journals. The entire machinery of his intellect is mobilized to escape the fundamental contradiction of existence. His struggle is made all the more frantic because he catches periodic glimpses of its futility, privately confessing that neither religious piety nor holy dread can bring him lasting peace. Through a tortured sleight of hand, he clothes the irrational in the garments of the absurd, projecting onto God the very attributes of earthly meaninglessness: injustice, incoherence, and incomprehensibility. His intellect operates solely to strangle the legitimate demands of the human spirit. For once reason is abandoned and nothing can be proven, anything whatsoever can be asserted as truth.

Abbé Galiani's maxim: 'The point is not to be cured, but to live with one's ailments.' Kierkegaard commits philosophical suicide because he cannot bear the tension; he frantically demands a cure, baptizing cosmic incoherence as God so that he can worship it.

Indeed, Kierkegaard himself shows us the path taken. It is the leitmotiv of the Journal. “What I lacked was the animal which also belongs to human destiny.… But give me a body then.” And further on: “Oh! especially in my early youth what should I not have given to be a man, even for six months … what I lack, basically, is a body and the physical conditions of existence.” Elsewhere, the same man nevertheless adopts the great cry of hope that has come down through so many centuries and quickened so many hearts, except that of the absurd man. “But for the Christian death is certainly not the end of everything and it implies infinitely more hope than life implies for us, even when that life is overflowing with health and vigor.” Reconciliation through scandal is still reconciliation. But even if fellow-feeling inclines one toward that attitude, still it must be said that excess justifies nothing. That transcends, as the saying goes, the human scale; therefore it must be superhuman. But this “therefore” is superfluous. There is no logical certainty here. There is no experimental probability either. All I can say is that, in fact, that transcends my scale. If I do not draw a negation from it, at least I do not want to found anything on the incomprehensible. I want to know whether I can live with what I know and with that alone. I am told again that here the intelligence must sacrifice its pride and the reason bow down. But if I recognize the limits of the reason, I do not therefore negate it, recognizing its relative powers. I merely want to remain in this middle path where the intelligence can remain clear. If that is its pride, I see no sufficient reason for giving it up. Nothing more profound, for example, than Kierkegaard’s view according to which despair is not a fact but a state: the very state of sin. For sin is what alienates from God. The absurd, which is the metaphysical state of the conscious man, does not lead to God. Perhaps this notion will become clearer if I risk this shocking statement: the absurd is sin without God.

'For the Christian,' he writes, 'death is by no means the end of all things; it promises infinitely more hope than mortal life could ever offer, even when that life overflows with vitality and vigor.' All I can legitimately state is that the mystery exceeds my mortal grasp. While I cannot disprove the transcendent, I flatly refuse to construct a philosophy upon the incomprehensible. I want to discover whether I can live exclusively with what I know, and with nothing more. I am warned once again that here intellect must abandon its pride and bow before the sacred. Yet recognizing the boundaries of human reason does not mean denying its real, relative power within human experience. I simply choose to walk this middle ridge where consciousness can maintain radical clarity. If that insistence is called intellectual pride, I see no valid reason to renounce it. Consider, for instance, Kierkegaard's brilliant insight that despair is not an isolated event, but a chronic spiritual condition: the exact state of sin. In Christian theology, sin is whatever alienates the creature from God. Yet the Absurd—which is the inescapable condition of the conscious human being—leads nowhere near God. Perhaps the concept becomes unmistakable if I venture this definition: the Absurd is sin without God.

I will focus specifically on the concept of 'intentionality,' made prominent by Edmund Husserl and the phenomenologists. I have already touched upon it. In its initial formulation, Husserl's method directly challenges the classical operations of rationalism. Let me restate the principle: thinking does not mean synthesizing or forcing appearances under some grand metaphysical umbrella. To think is to learn anew how to see, to direct one's attention, to transform every perceptual experience into a privileged moment of awareness. In other words, phenomenology refuses to explain the universe; it aims solely to describe lived experience as it actually appears. It reinforces the absurd mind in its fundamental axiom: there is no universal Truth, only localized truths. From the cool evening breeze to this hand resting upon my shoulder, every single phenomenon possesses its own distinct reality. Consciousness does not invent reality; it illuminates it simply by attending to it. The mind does not construct the object of its knowledge; it focuses like a lens, acting as pure attention—resembling, in Henri Bergson's metaphor, a magic lantern spotlighting a slide. The difference is that there is no overarching screenplay, only an unfolding sequence of disparate, disconnected images. Inside that magic lantern, every projection holds equal dignity. Consciousness suspends its chosen objects within lived experience. Through this act of focus, it isolates them from the background. Henceforth, they stand beyond all reductive metaphysical judgments. This is the 'intentionality' that defines consciousness. The term carries no implication of cosmic purpose or ultimate teleology. It designates pure mental orientation: its function is entirely descriptive and topographical.

Phenomenology's initial promise. Husserl's concept of intentionality initially appears compatible with the Absurd: it rejects grand metaphysical unifications, replaces universal 'Truth' with localized 'truths', and restricts itself to describing lived experience (the magic lantern).

The truth involved then for each of those aspects is psychological in nature. It simply testifies to the “interest” that reality can offer. It is a way of awaking a sleeping world and of making it vivid to the mind. But if one attempts to extend and give a rational basis to that notion of truth, if one claims to discover in this way the “essence” of each object of knowledge, one restores its depth to experience. For an absurd mind that is incomprehensible. Now, it is this wavering between modesty and assurance that is noticeable in the intentional attitude, and this shimmering of phenomenological thought will illustrate the absurd reasoning better than anything else. For Husserl speaks likewise of “extra-temporal essences” brought to light by the intention, and he sounds like Plato. All things are not explained by one thing but by all things. I see no difference. To be sure, those ideas or those essences that consciousness “effectuates” at the end of every description are not yet to be considered perfect models. But it is asserted that they are directly present in each datum of perception. There is no longer a single idea explaining everything, but an infinite number of essences giving a meaning to an infinite number of objects. The world comes to a stop, but also lights up. Platonic realism becomes intuitive, but it is still realism. Kierkegaard was swallowed up in his God; Parmenides plunged thought into the One. But here thought hurls itself into an abstract polytheism. But this is not all: hallucinations and fictions likewise belong to “extra-temporal essences.” In the new world of ideas, the species of centaurs collaborates with the more modest species of metropolitan man.

It simply catalogues what it cannot transcend. It demonstrates that even without a grand unifying principle, the human mind can still take joy in observing and clarifying every facet of experience. The truth belonging to each phenomenon remains strictly psychological. It simply bears witness to the fascinating texture that reality presents to our senses. It awakens a somnolent world, making it burst into vivid life before the mind. But the moment one attempts to universalize that insight—claiming to extract an eternal 'essence' from every perceived object—one smuggles metaphysical depth back into existence. To the lucid absurd mind, that move is completely unjustifiable. This perpetual oscillation between empirical modesty and dogmatic certainty defines phenomenology, and this intellectual double-dealing provides the clearest possible case study in philosophical suicide. For when Husserl begins speaking of 'extra-temporal essences' uncovered by intentionality, he sounds indistinguishable from Plato. Whether reality is explained by a single supreme Form or by an infinity of Forms makes zero practical difference. The metaphysical trap is identical. Admittedly, the essences that consciousness isolates through description are not presented as transcendent heavenly archetypes. Yet Husserl claims they are eternally present within every single perceptual datum. Instead of one monistic Idea explaining reality, we are given an infinite pantheon of eternal essences conferring meaning upon an infinite catalog of objects. The physical world is arrested in freeze-frame, bathed in artificial metaphysical light. Platonic realism has been made intuitive, but it remains Platonic realism. Kierkegaard drowned consciousness in his God; Parmenides dissolved it into the cosmic One. Husserl hurls thought into an abstract polytheism. Worse still, hallucinations, dreams, and imaginary creatures are granted their own 'extra-temporal essences.' In this bizarre intellectual heaven, the mythical species of centaurs enjoys equal metaphysical standing with the ordinary office worker.

They would therefore remain fully valid even if no conscious mind existed.' Even if consciousness did not exist, the laws of consciousness would still endure! From the abstract god of Husserl to the dazzling god of Kierkegaard the distance is not so great. Reason and the irrational lead to the same preaching. In truth the way matters but little; the will to arrive suffices. The abstract philosopher and the religious philosopher start out from the same disorder and support each other in the same anxiety. But the essential is to explain. Nostalgia is stronger here than knowledge. It is significant that the thought of the epoch is at once one of the most deeply imbued with a philosophy of the non-significance of the world and one of the most divided in its conclusions. It is constantly oscillating between extreme rationalization of reality which tends to break up that thought into standard reasons and its extreme irrationalization which tends to deify it. But this divorce is only apparent. It is a matter of reconciliation, and, in both cases, the leap suffices. It is always wrongly thought that the notion of reason is a one-way notion. To tell the truth, however rigorous it may be in its ambition, this concept is nonetheless just as unstable as others. Reason bears a quite human aspect, but it also is able to turn toward the divine. Since Plotinus, who was the first to reconcile it with the eternal climate, it has learned to turn away from the most cherished of its principles, which is contradiction, in order to integrate into it the strangest, the quite magic one of participation. It is an instrument of thought and not thought itself. Above all, a man’s thought is his nostalgia.

There is no reason to be astonished by the apparent paradox that drives thought to its own destruction through two opposite avenues: humiliated reason and triumphant reason. From Husserl's abstract deity to Kierkegaard's blinding God, the distance is remarkably short. Dogmatic rationalism and religious irrationalism arrive at the exact same sermon. In truth, the path chosen hardly matters; the desperate urge to arrive at a comforting conclusion is all that counts. The abstract metaphysician and the religious existentialist set out from the identical existential rupture, sustained by the same underlying panic. For both, the absolute imperative is to find an ultimate explanation. In both camps, existential nostalgia proves far stronger than lucid intellect. It is deeply revealing that modern philosophy is simultaneously saturated with the meaninglessness of the cosmos and bitterly divided in its ultimate conclusions. It swings continuously between the radical rationalization of reality (which atomizes the world into eternal concepts) and its radical irrationalization (which turns cosmic silence into a god). Yet that philosophical divide is purely cosmetic. Both sides seek reconciliation at any cost—and in both cases, the leap of faith accomplishes the trick. We mistakenly assume that reason functions as a rigid, one-way mechanism. In truth, no matter how rigorous its pretensions, human reason is just as malleable and volatile as any other mental faculty. Reason possesses an earthy, human dimension, yet it can just as easily be bent toward the divine. Ever since Plotinus first married reason to the eternal, intellect has learned to abandon its most essential anchor—the law of non-contradiction—in order to embrace the mystical, quasi-magical doctrine of participation in the One. Reason is merely an instrument of consciousness, not consciousness itself. And above all else, human thought is driven by its homesickness for unity.

Kierkegaard claims on his own terms that a single encounter with the boundary is enough to abolish that anguish through faith. But the absurd refuses to make that leap. For the absurd mind, the boundary applies exclusively to the overreaching ambitions of human intellect. The concept of the irrational, as brandished by the existentialists, is merely reason panicking, losing its nerve, and escaping through self-annihilation. The Absurd, in stark contrast, is lucid reason dispassionately mapping its own limits.

The Philosophical Move

The Definitive Distinction: Panic vs. Radical Clarity. Existential irrationalism is reason becoming confused and killing itself in terror. The Absurd, by contrast, is lucid reason calmly establishing its own boundaries without fleeing into faith or despair.

The Refusal of Preaching. Comparing the absurd demand with the offers of Husserl and Kierkegaard, Camus rejects both. The absurd man's sole 'sin' is wanting to know—a hunger he refuses to trade for theological consolations or phenomenological word games.

It was a matter of living and thinking with those dislocations, of knowing whether one had to accept or refuse. There can be no question of masking the evidence, of suppressing the absurd by denying one of the terms of its equation. It is essential to know whether one can live with it or whether, on the other hand, logic commands one to die of it. I am not interested in philosophical suicide, but rather in plain suicide. I merely wish to purge it of its emotional content and know its logic and its integrity. Any other position implies for the absurd mind deceit and the mind’s retreat before what the mind itself has brought to light. Husserl claims to obey the desire to escape “the inveterate habit of living and thinking in certain well-known and convenient conditions of existence,” but the final leap restores in him the eternal and its comfort. The leap does not represent an extreme danger as Kierkegaard would like it to do. The danger, on the contrary, lies in the subtle instant that precedes the leap. Being able to remain on that dizzying crest—that is integrity and the rest is subterfuge. I know also that never has helplessness inspired such striking harmonies as those of Kierkegaard. But if helplessness has its place in the indifferent landscapes of history, it has none in a reasoning whose exigence is now known.

Kierkegaard suffocates my longing, while Husserl artificially reassembles the universe. That is not what I was seeking. The task was to learn how to live and think within these profound fractures—to determine whether one must accept the condition or reject it. There can be no question of obscuring the evidence, or of erasing the absurd by eliminating one of the terms in its equation. The vital question is whether one can live with this tension, or whether, on the contrary, rigorous logic commands one to die of it. I have zero interest in philosophical suicide; my sole concern is with literal suicide. I simply want to strip the act of its emotional sentimentality, discovering its underlying logic and philosophical integrity. Any other posture represents intellectual cowardice—a shameful retreat by the mind before the very realities it has uncovered. Husserl claims to break free from 'the ingrained habit of living and thinking within conventional, comfortable conditions of existence'—yet his final leap restores the tranquil comfort of eternity. Nor does the leap constitute an act of heroic daring, as Kierkegaard so desperately wanted to believe. The true danger, on the contrary, resides in that razor-thin instant that immediately precedes the leap. Possessing the strength to maintain one's balance upon that dizzying ridge—that alone is intellectual integrity; everything else is evasion. I know, too, that human helplessness has never inspired such haunting, magnificent prose as that of Kierkegaard. Yet while tragic helplessness may claim its rightful place across the indifferent expanse of human history, it has no place in an argument whose rigorous demands are now clearly understood.

The Philosophical Move

The Dizzying Ridge (Camus's Manifesto of Integrity). Refusing both Kierkegaard's leap and Husserl's Platonism, Camus stands on the narrow ledge before the leap. True courage is not leaping into faith, but holding one's ground on the dizzying crest of the Absurd without hope and without surrender.

Now the main thing is done, I hold certain facts from which I cannot separate. What I know, what is certain, what I cannot deny, what I cannot reject—this is what counts. I can negate everything of that part of me that lives on vague nostalgias, except this desire for unity, this longing to solve, this need for clarity and cohesion. I can refute everything in this world surrounding me that offends or enraptures me, except this chaos, this sovereign chance and this divine equivalence which springs from anarchy. I don’t know whether this world has a meaning that transcends it. But I know that I do not know that meaning and that it is impossible for me just now to know it. What can a meaning outside my condition mean to me? I can understand only in human terms. What I touch, what resists me—that is what I understand. And these two certainties—my appetite for the absolute and for unity and the impossibility of reducing this world to a rational and reasonable principle—I also know that I cannot reconcile them. What other truth can I admit without lying, without bringing in a hope I lack and which means nothing within the limits of my condition?

The primary work is finished; I now possess several undeniable facts from which I cannot separate myself. What I know, what is certain, what I can neither deny nor discard—this alone matters. I can dismiss every part of myself that feeds on vague nostalgia, except for this persistent hunger for unity, this drive to resolve, this demand for clarity and coherence. I can reject everything in this surrounding world that offends or delights me, except for this prevailing chaos, this sovereign randomness, and this cosmic indifference born of pure anarchy. Whether this world possesses a transcendent meaning beyond itself, I do not know. I only know that I am ignorant of such meaning, and that within my current existence it is impossible for me to grasp it. What could a meaning that lies entirely outside my human condition possibly signify to me? I can comprehend reality only in human terms. What my hands touch, what pushes back against me—that is what I understand. And between these two foundational certainties—my appetite for absolute unity and the impossibility of reducing this world to a rational principle—I know there can be no reconciliation. What other truth could I accept without lying, without introducing an unfounded hope that means nothing within the boundaries of my mortal condition?

The Philosophical Move

Camus consolidates his epistemological baseline: the twin irreducible poles of the Absurd. Human consciousness demands absolute unity and rational coherence, while the empirical universe presents only silence, randomness, and resistance. Rejecting any metaphysical leap to bridge this gap, he insists on honesty over consoling fictions.

I cannot cross it out with a stroke of the pen. What I believe to be true I must therefore preserve. What seems to me so obvious, even against me, I must support. And what constitutes the basis of that conflict, of that break between the world and my mind, but the awareness of it? If therefore I want to preserve it, I can through a constant awareness, ever revived, ever alert. This is what, for the moment, I must remember. At this moment the absurd, so obvious and yet so hard to win, returns to a man’s life and finds its home there. At this moment, too, the mind can leave the arid, dried-up path of lucid effort. That path now emerges in daily life. It encounters the world of the anonymous impersonal pronoun “one,” but henceforth man enters in with his revolt and his lucidity. He has forgotten how to hope. This hell of the present is his Kingdom at last. All problems recover their sharp edge. Abstract evidence retreats before the poetry of forms and colors. Spiritual conflicts become embodied and return to the abject and magnificent shelter of man’s heart. None of them is settled. But all are transfigured. Is one going to die, escape by the leap, rebuild a mansion of ideas and forms to one’s own scale? Is one, on the contrary, going to take up the heart-rending and marvelous wager of the absurd? Let’s make a final effort in this regard and draw all our conclusions. The body, affection, creation, action, human nobility will then resume their places in this mad world. At last man will again find there the wine of the absurd and the bread of indifference on which he feeds his greatness.

What appears undeniable, even when it works against me, I must uphold. And what sustains this conflict, this fracture between the world and my intellect, except my active awareness of it? If I wish to preserve this tension, I can do so only through an unyielding, wakeful consciousness that is constantly renewed. This is the principle I must keep firmly in mind. At this juncture, the absurd—at once glaringly evident and yet so difficult to attain—reenters human life and makes its home there. Here, too, the intellect can depart from the dry, abstract desert of mere logical exercise. That path now opens out into the concrete reality of everyday life. It encounters the anonymous world of the crowd, yet from now on a man enters that world armed with his conscious defiance and his radical clarity. He has forgotten how to indulge in hope. This purgatory of the immediate present has become his kingdom. Every dilemma regains its razor-sharp intensity. Bloodless abstractions give way to the vibrant poetry of physical shapes and colors. Metaphysical struggles take on flesh, returning to that wretched yet magnificent sanctuary: the human heart. Not a single conflict is resolved. Yet every one of them is transfigured. Shall we choose death, escape through an intellectual leap of faith, or construct an artificial palace of theories tailored to our own comfort? Or shall we, on the contrary, take up the agonizing and magnificent wager of the absurd? Let us make one final effort to follow this reasoning through and draw all its consequences. The physical body, human affection, artistic creation, decisive action, and human dignity will then reclaim their rightful places in this irrational world. At last, man will rediscover the wine of the absurd and the bread of indifference upon which he nourishes his greatness.

The Philosophical Move

The Tree and Cat thought experiment illustrates human exile from nature. Consciousness separates humanity from unthinking immersion in the cosmos. Rather than remaining an abstract exercise, the absurd descends into daily life, transforming the immediate present into man's kingdom, where no tension is dissolved but all experience is illuminated.

He is assured that this is the sin of pride, but he does not understand the notion of sin; that perhaps hell is in store, but he has not enough imagination to visualize that strange future; that he is losing immortal life, but that seems to him an idle consideration. Hence, what he demands of himself is to live solely with what he knows, to accommodate himself to what is, and to bring in nothing that is not certain. He is told that nothing is. But this at least is a certainty. And it is with this that he is concerned: he wants to find out if it is possible to live without appeal.

Let us emphasize the method once more: everything depends upon persistence. At a certain stage of his journey, the absurd man faces severe temptation. History offers an abundance of religions and self-styled prophets, even secular ones without gods. They all urge him to take the leap. They warn him that this refusal is the sin of intellectual pride, yet the concept of sin is meaningless to him; they threaten that damnation awaits, but he lacks the credulity to picture such a bizarre future; they caution that he forfeits eternal life, but that strikes him as an idle distraction. They demand that he confess his guilt. Instead, he feels entirely innocent. In truth, that is all he experiences: his irremediable, radical innocence. And it is this innocence that grants him complete freedom. Consequently, what he requires of himself is to live exclusively by what he knows, to adapt himself to what actually exists, and to introduce nothing that lacks certainty. He is told that nothing is certain. Yet that absence of certainty is itself a definitive fact. This is his sole preoccupation: he wants to discover whether it is possible to live without appeal to any higher authority.

The Philosophical Move

Living 'without appeal' (vivre sans appel). Confronted with religious and secular calls for a leap of faith, the absurd man claims 'irreparable innocence.' Denying the dogmatic categories of original sin and transcendent guilt, he refuses any palliative that cannot be verified by immediate human experience.

Now I can broach the notion of suicide. It has already been felt what solution might be given. At this point the problem is reversed. It was previously a question of finding out whether or not life had to have a meaning to be lived. It now becomes clear, on the contrary, that it will be lived all the better if it has no meaning. Living an experience, a particular fate, is accepting it fully. Now, no one will live this fate, knowing it to be absurd, unless he does everything to keep before him that absurd brought to light by consciousness. Negating one of the terms of the opposition on which he lives amounts to escaping it. To abolish conscious revolt is to elude the problem. The theme of permanent revolution is thus carried into individual experience. Living is keeping the absurd alive. Keeping it alive is, above all, contemplating it. Unlike Eurydice, the absurd dies only when we turn away from it. One of the only coherent philosophical positions is thus revolt. It is a constant confrontation between man and his own obscurity. It is an insistence upon an impossible transparency. It challenges the world anew every second. Just as danger provided man the unique opportunity of seizing awareness, so metaphysical revolt extends awareness to the whole of experience. It is that constant presence of man in his own eyes. It is not aspiration, for it is devoid of hope. That revolt is the certainty of a crushing fate, without the resignation that ought to accompany it.

I can now address the question of suicide directly. The direction of the answer has already become apparent. At this critical juncture, the terms of the problem are reversed. Earlier, the question was whether life required an overarching purpose in order to be worth living. Now it becomes evident, on the contrary, that life will be lived far more fully precisely because it has no ultimate meaning. To undergo an experience, to inhabit a particular destiny, means accepting it without reservation. Yet no one can truly inhabit this fate, knowing it to be absurd, unless he makes every effort to keep that absurdity constantly visible before his conscious mind. To destroy either term of the tension that sustains him is simply an attempt to run away. To extinguish conscious defiance is to evade the fundamental problem. The ideal of permanent revolution is thereby translated into individual existence. To live is to keep the absurd alive. And to keep the absurd alive is, above all else, to look it directly in the face. Unlike Eurydice, the absurd perishes only when we avert our eyes. Thus, one of the few genuinely coherent philosophical stances is defiant revolt. It is an unending confrontation between man and his own inner darkness. It is a persistent demand for an impossible transparency. It interrogates the universe afresh at every passing second. Just as imminent physical peril offers a person a rare flash of heightened consciousness, so metaphysical defiance extends that lucidity across the whole breadth of experience. It is humanity standing continually face to face with itself. It is not an upward aspiration, because it is stripped of all hope. That defiance is the absolute certainty of a crushing fate, maintained entirely without the resignation that usually accompanies it.

The Philosophical Move

The Dialectical Inversion. Camus reverses the initial premise: life is lived better without meaning. To live an absurd fate requires sustaining the tension between consciousness and cosmic silence. Suicide abolishes one term and destroys the encounter. Defiant revolt (the first consequence) is keeping the absurd alive like a permanent inner revolution.

To ask whether man is free is ultimately to ask whether he must submit to a cosmic master. The peculiar absurdity of this theological dilemma lies in the fact that the very postulate that makes divine freedom imaginable simultaneously strips human freedom of all coherence. In the presence of God, the question ceases to be about human freedom and becomes the problem of evil. The classic dilemma is well known: either we are unfree, and an omnipotent God is the author of evil; or we are free and morally responsible, in which case God is not all-powerful. Centuries of scholastic hairsplitting have neither sharpened nor softened the severity of that contradiction.

No matter how detached one tries to remain from social and moral dogmas, one is inevitably influenced by them, and one shapes one's daily life around even the most admirable of them. The absurd man thus recognizes that he was never genuinely free. To put it plainly: to the extent that I invest in hope, obsess over discovering some personal destiny, or attempt to curate my existence to prove it possesses meaning, I construct the very prison walls that enclose me. I become like those bureaucrats of the intellect and the heart who inspire in me only revulsion—whose fatal error, I now see clearly, was to take human metaphysical freedom seriously.

Yes, indeed, but not that night that is born under closed eyelids and through the mere will of man—dark, impenetrable night that the mind calls up in order to plunge into it. If it must encounter a night, let it be rather that of despair, which remains lucid—polar night, vigil of the mind, whence will arise perhaps that white and virginal brightness which outlines every object in the light of the intelligence. At that degree, equivalence encounters passionate understanding. Then it is no longer even a question of judging the existential leap. It resumes its place amid the age-old fresco of human attitudes. For the spectator, if he is conscious, that leap is still absurd. In so far as it thinks it solves the paradox, it reinstates it intact. On this score, it is stirring. On this score, everything resumes its place and the absurd world is reborn in all its splendor and diversity.

Undoubtedly—yet not that artificial darkness conjured behind deliberately shut eyelids by a willful act of self-delusion, an impenetrable gloom that the mind invents solely to drown itself in comforting ignorance. If the intellect must face the darkness, let it be the night of lucid despair: a polar night, a vigilant watch of the mind, from which may rise that stark, immaculate dawn throwing every contour into the sharp relief of intelligence. At this altitude, cosmic indifference meets passionate comprehension. At that point, it is no longer even necessary to pass judgment upon the existential leap of faith. It simply reassumes its place among the ancient tapestry of human compromises. To the lucid observer, that leap remains thoroughly absurd. In believing that it solves the paradox, it leaves the contradiction entirely intact. In that very futility, it retains a tragic grandeur. And on these terms, every element reclaims its rightful place, and the absurd universe is reborn in all its richness and diversity.

As a modern author writes, “it is not essential to be a dupe.” The attitudes of which I shall treat can assume their whole meaning only through consideration of their contraries. Otherwise, that has no importance: a man’s failures imply judgment, not of circumstances, but of himself. I am choosing solely men who aim only to expend themselves or whom I see to be expending themselves. That has no further implications. For the moment I want to speak only of a world in which thoughts, like lives, are devoid of future. Everything that makes man work and get excited utilizes hope. The sole thought that is not mendacious is therefore a sterile thought. In the absurd world the value of a notion or of a life is measured by its sterility.

As a modern writer observed, "One is not obliged to be a fool." The ways of living I am about to examine derive their full significance only when contrasted with their opposites. Certain experiences either serve a person or do them a disservice. They serve a person only if they remain fully conscious of them. Otherwise, the circumstance matters little: a person’s failure reflects not on external conditions, but on themselves. I select here only individuals whose sole aim is to burn through their vitality, or who visibly expend their lives without reservation. That choice implies nothing beyond itself. For now, I wish to speak only of a world where thoughts, like human lives, possess no future. Everything that drives human labor and ambition depends on the illusion of hope. The only thought that does not lie, therefore, is a sterile thought. Within an absurd world, the true value of an idea—or of a life—is measured precisely by its refusal to bear fruit for an imagined future.

The Post-Office Clerk and the Conqueror. Camus establishes the premise of Part II: social status and worldly grandeur are irrelevant illusions. Dignity depends entirely on lucid awareness. Authentic existential living demands thought and action devoid of hope—measuring life by conscious expenditure rather than future dividends.

Is Don Juan melancholy? This is not likely. I shall barely have recourse to the legend. That laugh, the conquering insolence, that playfulness and love of the theater are all clear and joyous. Every healthy creature tends to multiply himself. So it is with Don Juan. But, furthermore, melancholy people have two reasons for being so: they don’t know or they hope. Don Juan knows and does not hope. He reminds one of those artists who know their limits, never go beyond them, and in that precarious interval in which they take their spiritual stand enjoy all the wonderful ease of masters. And that is indeed genius: the intelligence that knows its frontiers. Up to the frontier of physical death Don Juan is ignorant of melancholy. The moment he knows, his laugh bursts forth and makes one forgive everything. He was melancholy at the time when he hoped. Is Don Juan a melancholic figure? That is highly unlikely. We hardly need to consult romantic legends to see this. His laughter, his triumphant audacity, his sheer delight in performance and theatricality are entirely radiant and joyful. Every healthy, vital organism naturally seeks to multiply itself; so it is with Don Juan. Moreover, people fall into melancholy for only two reasons: either they are ignorant of reality, or they cling to hope. Don Juan knows reality completely, and he harbors no hope. He resembles those accomplished artists who recognize their exact boundaries, never exceed them, and within that narrow, precarious space where they take their stand, command all the graceful mastery of genius. And that is true genius: an intellect fully conscious of its frontiers. Right up to the boundary of physical death, Don Juan remains untouched by melancholy. The moment clarity dawns on him, his laughter rings out, sweeping away all reproach. He was melancholy only back when he still clung to hope. Today, upon the lips of the woman before him, he tastes the astringent, bracing flavor of the only knowledge that exists. Bitter? Hardly—merely that essential imperfection that renders human happiness tangible.

The Philosophical Move

Melancholy Belongs to Hope, Not Lucidity. Melancholy is born from two sources: ignorance of mortal limits or agonizing longing for an eternity. Don Juan eliminates both. Don Juan vs. Faust (The Refusal of Transcendent Bargains). Faust is an intellectual who secretly believes in the absolute and trades his soul out of spiritual impotence. Molina's line ('What a long respite you grant me!') anchors his focus on the concrete span of life.

I find it even easier to accept the historical tradition in which Don Juan ends his days secluded inside a monastery. Not that the pious moral of the story holds any water: what possible sanctuary could he ask from a God he does not believe in? What refuge could he conceivably seek from a deity he has always denied? Rather, this cloister represents the ultimate logical denouement of an existence steeped in the absurd—the austere finale of a life devoted exclusively to fleeting pleasures. At this threshold, extreme sensuality folds into extreme asceticism. One must understand that these two extremes are merely opposite faces of the identical existential poverty. What more haunting spectacle could one imagine than a man betrayed by his aging flesh, who—simply because he failed to die in the prime of life—plays out the theatrical farce to the very end: confronting a God he does not worship, performing religious rituals with the same mechanical detachment with which he once pursued seduction, kneeling before an absolute void, with arms outstretched toward a silent heaven he knows to be utterly devoid of depth?

The Philosophical Move

The Stone Commander Never Came: The Desolation of Being Right. The greatest existential insight in the essay: the terrifying realization is not that God punishes the rebel, but that God never appears. Seduction and monastic asceticism are two sides of the same coin: living fully within physical reality without transcendent illusions. Don Juan kneeling in an empty chapel before a silent void is the ultimate absurd hero.

Part II: The Absurd Man

6. Drama

Original 1955 Translation Page 64 • §1 of 12

“The play’s the thing,” says Hamlet, “wherein I’ll catch the conscience of the king.” “Catch” is indeed the word. For conscience moves swiftly or withdraws within itself. It has to be caught on the wing, at that barely perceptible moment when it glances fleetingly at itself. The everyday man does not enjoy tarrying. Everything, on the contrary, hurries him onward. But at the same time nothing interests him more than himself, especially his potentialities. Whence his interest in the theater, in the show, where so many fates are offered him, where he can accept the poetry without feeling the sorrow. There at least can be recognized the thoughtless man, and he continues to hasten toward some hope or other. The absurd man begins where that one leaves off, where, ceasing to admire the play, the mind wants to enter in. Entering into all these lives, experiencing them in their diversity, amounts to acting them out. I am not saying that actors in general obey that impulse, that they are absurd men, but that their fate is an absurd fate which might charm and attract a lucid heart. It is necessary to establish this in order to grasp without misunderstanding what will follow.

Dignified Modern Translation Page 64•§1 of 12 (8%)

"The play's the thing," declares Hamlet, "wherein I'll catch the conscience of the King." "Catch" is precisely the right word. For consciousness moves with extreme speed, or retreats instantly back into itself. It must be captured mid-flight, at that fleeting, almost imperceptible instant when it casts a backward glance upon its own reflection. The ordinary person has no patience for lingering self-examination. On the contrary, the momentum of daily life relentlessly drives them forward. Yet at the same time, nothing fascinates a person more than themselves—especially their own unrealized possibilities. Hence their enduring attraction to the theater, to the stage, where countless alternative destinies are laid out before them, allowing them to savor the dramatic beauty without bearing the actual weight of the agony. In that passive spectator one recognizes the unreflective person, perpetually rushing toward one comforting hope after another. The absurd man begins precisely where that spectator stops: where, refusing to remain a mere detached observer, the mind demands to enter the arena directly. To inhabit all these varied human lives, experiencing them in their full multiplicity, is to perform them on the stage. I am not claiming that actors as a class consciously obey this philosophical imperative, or that they are personally absurd heroes; rather, their professional destiny is inherently an absurd destiny—one capable of fascinating and attracting a lucid mind. This distinction must be established clearly from the outset to avoid any confusion in what follows.

The Philosophical Move

The Spectator vs. The Actor (Passive Illusion vs. Active Embodiment). Everyday humans use theater as escapism: an effortless peek into alternate lives without personal risk or suffering. The absurd person, however, refuses passive spectatorship. By physically embodying multiple characters, the actor transforms the quantitative appetite of the absurd into physical reality, living multiple lifetimes in an afternoon.

The actor's domain is the kingdom of the fleeting. Of all forms of celebrity, theatrical fame is acknowledged to be the most ephemeral. At least, that is the common platitude. Viewed from the cosmic perspective of Sirius, even Goethe's masterpieces will be reduced to dust in ten thousand years, and his name will be utterly erased. Contemplated with seriousness, it dissolves our petty anxieties into the dignified nobility of existential indifference. Above all, it turns our attention toward the only certainty we possess: the immediate present. Of all varieties of fame, the least deceptive is the fame that is directly experienced in the flesh.

The Philosophical Move

Cosmic Indifference (The Perspective of Sirius). Intellectuals boast of posthumous immortality through books and monuments. Camus invokes the cosmic scale (the star Sirius) to show that all art and human memory will perish. The actor's fame is the most honest because it does not pretend to outlive its performance; it is expended and enjoyed entirely in real time.

A writer has some hope even if he is not appreciated. He assumes that his works will bear witness to what he was. At best the actor will leave us a photograph, and nothing of what he was himself, his gestures and his silences, his gasping or his panting with love, will come down to us. For him, not to be known is not to act, and not acting is dying a hundred times with all the creatures he would have brought to life or resuscitated.

The actor has therefore chosen an immediate, collective glory—a fame affirmed and experienced night after night before a living audience. From the undeniable truth that everything must eventually perish, he derives the most rigorous conclusion. For the actor, success or failure is instantaneous: he either triumphs in the room or he fails completely. A writer can always nurse the secret hope of future recognition even when neglected in his lifetime, assuming his written pages will testify to posterity on his behalf. At best, the actor leaves behind a lifeless photograph; nothing of his living essence—his sudden physical gestures, his pregnant pauses, his breath catching in grief or panting with desire—can ever be preserved. For the actor, not to be recognized in the moment is not to perform at all; and not performing means dying a hundred deaths alongside every character he was poised to ignite into life.

The Philosophical Move

A mime of the ephemeral, the actor trains and perfects himself only in appearances. The theatrical convention is that the heart expresses itself and communicates itself only through gestures and in the body—or through the voice, which is as much of the soul as of the body. The rule of that art insists that everything be magnified and translated into flesh. If it were essential on the stage to love as people really love, to employ that irreplaceable voice of the heart, to look as people contemplate in life, our speech would be in code. But here silences must make themselves heard. Love speaks up louder, and immobility itself becomes spectacular. The body is king. Not everyone can be “theatrical,” and this unjustly maligned word covers a whole æsthetic and a whole ethic. Half a man’s life is spent in implying, in turning away, and in keeping silent. Here the actor is the intruder. He breaks the spell chaining that soul, and at last the passions can rush onto their stage. They speak in every gesture; they live only through shouts and cries. Thus the actor creates his characters for display. He outlines or sculptures them and slips into their imaginary form, transfusing his blood into their phantoms. I am of course speaking of great drama, the kind that gives the actor an opportunity to fulfill his wholly physical fate. Take Shakespeare, for instance. In that impulsive drama the physical passions lead the dance. They explain everything. Without them all would collapse. Never would King Lear keep the appointment set by madness without the brutal gesture that exiles Cordelia and condemns Edgar. It is just that the unfolding of that tragedy should thenceforth be dominated by madness. Souls are given over to the demons and their saraband. No fewer than four madmen: one by trade, another by intention, and the last two through suffering—four disordered bodies, four unutterable aspects of a single condition.

A pantomimist of the temporary, the actor refines his craft exclusively within the realm of surfaces and appearances. The fundamental rule of the stage is that the human heart can communicate its internal truth only through physical gesture and the living body—or through the human voice, which belongs equally to the flesh and to the spirit. The law of the theater dictates that every psychological nuance must be magnified and translated into physical reality. If an actor were to portray love on stage with the whispered murmurs of everyday life, using the mute glances of private domesticity, his performance would remain an indecipherable secret to the room. On stage, even silence must ring with audible force. Passion must speak with heightened volume, and complete immobility must become a gripping spectacle. The physical body reigns supreme. Not everyone possesses the talent to be "theatrical"—a word unfairly degraded, which in truth encompasses an entire aesthetic and moral philosophy. Ordinary human life is spent in hesitation, evasive glances, and stifled silences. The actor arrives on stage as a radical intruder. He shatters the paralytic spell binding the human soul, finally letting dormant passions storm the platform. Here, passions speak through muscular movement; they announce their reality through cries, physical confrontations, and declarations. In this way, the actor builds figures meant for public exposure. He chisels their silhouettes, slips into their ghostly contours, and transfuses his own warm blood into their fictional veins. I am speaking, of course, of classical tragedy—the kind of drama that permits an actor to realize his purely physical destiny. Consider Shakespeare. In his visceral theater, raw physical passions orchestrate the entire drama. They provide the sole engine of the narrative; without them, the architecture falls to pieces. King Lear would never arrive at his fatal rendezvous with madness on the storm-swept heath were it not for the impulsive, violent gestures with which he disowns Cordelia and banishes Edgar. It is entirely fitting that this catastrophic collapse should be ruled by lunacy. Souls are surrendered to chaotic furies and their frenzied dance. Shakespeare assembles no fewer than four distinct madmen: one a professional fool, one feigning insanity by design, and two driven mad through unbearable anguish—four shattered physical vessels embodying four unspeakable dimensions of a single human condition.

The Primacy of the Body in Drama (Shakespeare's Four Madmen). In normal life, humans hide behind polite restraint and repression. Contradictory impulses achieve physical reconciliation within him. He stands at the exact crossroads where intellect and biology fuse—where the mind, exhausted by abstract philosophical defeats, turns back toward its most dependable comrade: the body. The absurd man pushes the screen aside to look directly at the scaffold.

All is well, everything is permitted, and nothing is hateful—these are absurd judgments. But what an amazing creation in which those creatures of fire and ice seem so familiar to us.
