Before advancing, we must observe that Kirillov’s metaphysical rebellion reemerges in other characters who embody related absurd postures. Nikolai Stavrogin and Ivan Karamazov attempt to live out these absurd realizations in concrete action. They represent those who have been theoretically liberated by Kirillov’s sacrifice. They test their prowess at reigning as sovereign kings of their own lives. Stavrogin lives an existence of cold, corrosive irony—and its destructive fallout is infamous. He incites intense hatred everywhere he walks. Yet the definitive cipher to his soul appears in his final suicide note: 'I have never been capable of hating anything.' He is a sovereign king of pure indifference. Ivan Karamazov claims identical kingship by adamantly refusing to surrender the intellectual sovereignty of reason. To those who, like his saintly brother Alyosha, argue that one must humiliate human reason to accept faith, Ivan retorts that such spiritual surrender is shameful. His defining motto remains 'Everything is permitted'—tinged with an unmistakable undercurrent of melancholy. Inevitably, like Nietzsche—the most famous assassin of God—Ivan collapses into madness. Yet this is an occupational hazard of radical honesty, and confronted with such tragic ruins, the absurd mind simply asks: 'What does that prove?' Dostoevsky’s novels construct a ruthless logic pursued to the point of death: ecstasy, terrifying freedom, and the tragic majesty of mortals crowned as kings. 'All is well,' 'Everything is permitted,' and 'I can hate nothing'—these are quintessential absurd verdicts. Yet what a breathtaking imaginative triumph it is that these characters of fire and ice feel so intimately recognizable to us. The stormy universe of indifference churning within their breasts does not strike us as alien or monstrous. We recognize within their torment the magnified reflection of our own daily anxieties.

The absurd triumvirate: Kirillov (suicide to prove freedom), Stavrogin (sovereign indifference), and Ivan Karamazov ('Everything is permitted'). Their tragic ends (madness, suicide) do not refute their logic; they confirm the terrifying weight of lucidity.

Since this is the case, the immortality of the human soul exists without any doubt.” Then again in the last pages of his last novel, at the conclusion of that gigantic combat with God, some children ask Aliocha: “Karamazov, is it true what religion says, that we shall rise from the dead, that we shall see one another again?” And Aliocha answers: “Certainly, we shall see one another again, we shall joyfully tell one another everything that has happened.”

Yet where does Dostoevsky himself ultimately land? Two passages reveal the total metaphysical reversal through which the novelist retreats toward transcendent consolation. When his essay on logical suicide provoked furious outrage from contemporary critics, Dostoevsky clarified his stance in subsequent issues of the Diary, deducing: 'If faith in eternal life is so indispensable to human sanity that without it man is driven to destroy himself, then immortality must represent the natural, intended state of humanity.' 'Because this need is universal, the immortality of the human soul must exist beyond any shadow of a doubt.' And again, in the closing chapter of his final masterpiece, at the climax of that monumental wrestling match with God, schoolboys gather around Alyosha asking: 'Karamazov, is it true what faith teaches—that we will rise from the dead, that we will see each other again?' And Alyosha reassures them: 'Without question, we will see each other again, and we will joyfully recount everything that has happened.'

The author's philosophical retreat. Camus exposes Dostoevsky's intellectual leap of faith: arguing that because man cannot endure mortality without despair, immortality MUST exist (the pragmatic fallacy), culminating in Alyosha's promise of resurrection.

One commentator correctly pointed out that Dostoevsky is on Ivan’s side and that the affirmative chapters took three months of effort whereas what he called “the blasphemies” were written in three weeks in a state of excitement. There is not one of his characters who does not have that thorn in the flesh, who does not aggravate it or seek a remedy for it in sensation or immortality. In any case, let us remain with this doubt. Here is a work which, in a chiaroscuro more gripping than the light of day, permits us to seize man’s struggle against his hopes. Having reached the end, the creator makes his choice against his characters. That contradiction thus allows us to make a distinction. It is not an absurd work that is involved here, but a work that propounds the absurd problem.

Alyosha, by contrast, proclaims without hesitation: 'We will meet again.' Suicide and existential madness are banished from the horizon. Mankind failed to comprehend his sacrifice. Therefore, the writer speaking to us is not an absurd creator, but an existential novelist who executes a leap of faith. Reflecting upon The Brothers Karamazov, Dostoevsky admitted: 'The central question running through every page of this novel is the identical torment that has haunted my conscience all my life: the existence of God.' It is difficult to believe that the pages of a novel could magically transform the lifelong anguish of a titan into serene religious faith. A perceptive critic rightly observed that Dostoevsky's instinctive sympathy lay with Ivan: the pious refutations required three months of agonizing labor, whereas the fiery 'blasphemies' were drafted in three weeks of incandescent inspiration. Every single one of his characters carries that agonizing thorn in the flesh, inflaming the wound or seeking an antidote through sensory excess or dreams of eternity. Regardless, let us honor the unresolved tension of his struggle. We are left with a masterpiece whose chiaroscuro—more haunting than midday sun—captures the desperate combat between man and his own craving for hope. Arriving at the final crossroads, the creator sides against his own greatest creations. That crucial betrayal allows us to establish a vital aesthetic distinction. Dostoevsky's fiction is not an absurd work; it is a work that powerfully dramatizes the absurd problem only to flee from its conclusion.

The creator choosing against his characters. Dostoevsky's emotional genius was on the side of Ivan's blasphemies, but his theological terror forced a Christian resolution. It is a work that poses the absurd question with genius, but resolves it through an existential leap.

Part III: Absurd Creation

10. Ephemeral Creation

At this point I perceive, therefore, that hope cannot be eluded forever and that it can beset even those who wanted to be free of it. This is the interest I find in the works discussed up to this point. I could, at least in the realm of creation, list some truly absurd works. But everything must have a beginning. The object of this quest is a certain fidelity. The Church has been so harsh with heretics only because she deemed that there is no worse enemy than a child who has gone astray. But the record of Gnostic effronteries and the persistence of Manichean currents have contributed more to the construction of orthodox dogma than all the prayers. With due allowance, the same is true of the absurd. One recognizes one’s course by discovering the paths that stray from it. At the very conclusion of the absurd reasoning, in one of the attitudes dictated by its logic, it is not a matter of indifference to find hope coming back in under one of its most touching guises. That shows the difficulty of the absurd ascesis. Above all, it shows the necessity of unfailing alertness and thus confirms the general plan of this essay.

At this stage, I recognize that metaphysical hope cannot be evaded effortlessly, and that it can seduce even those who sought most fiercely to be free of it. This is precisely what makes the works analyzed so far profoundly illuminating. I could easily assemble, at least within the domain of art, a catalog of authentically absurd works. Yet every rigorous inquiry must begin at the foundation. The purpose of this entire investigation is an unwavering fidelity to truth. The Church dealt ruthlessly with heretics precisely because she understood that no enemy is more dangerous than an errant child of the faith. Yet the daring provocations of the Gnostics and the tenacity of Manichean currents contributed far more to forging orthodox Christian dogma than centuries of pious prayers. Allowing for differences of scale, the identical principle governs our study of the absurd. One defines the true path by charting every detour that wanders away from it. At the very culmination of absurd reasoning, within an artistic stance demanded by its own logic, it is deeply significant to watch hope slip back inside through one of its most touching disguises. This demonstrates the supreme difficulty of the absurd ascesis. Above all, it reveals why relentless mental alertness is indispensable, thereby confirming the architectural design of this essay.

The Philosophical Move

The dialectical function of heretics and deviations. Hope is an insidious gravity. Just as heresies defined orthodox church dogma, tracing how great artists (like Dostoevsky) retreat into hope illuminates the exacting discipline of maintaining absurd fidelity.

Original 1955 Translation Page 90 • §2 of 11

But if it is still too early to list absurd works, at least a conclusion can be reached as to the creative attitude, one of those which can complete absurd existence. Art can never be so well served as by a negative thought. Its dark and humiliated proceedings are as necessary to the understanding of a great work as black is to white. To work and create “for nothing,” to sculpture in clay, to know that one’s creation has no future, to see one’s work destroyed in a day while being aware that fundamentally this has no more importance than building for centuries—this is the difficult wisdom that absurd thought sanctions. Performing these two tasks simultaneously, negating on the one hand and magnifying on the other, is the way open to the absurd creator. He must give the void its colors.

While it may be premature to compile a definitive canon of absurd art, we can at least reach a clear conclusion regarding the creative stance—one of the vital disciplines that completes an absurd existence. Art has never been so powerfully vitalized as by a philosophy of conscious refusal. Its austere, humbled methods are as indispensable to grasping a genuine masterpiece as darkness is to revealing light. The whole art of Kafka consists in forcing the reader to reread. His endings, or his absence of endings, suggest explanations which, however, are not revealed in clear language but, before they seem justified, require that the story be reread from another point of view. Sometimes there is a double possibility of interpretation, whence appears the necessity for two readings. This is what the author wanted. But it would be wrong to try to interpret everything in Kafka in detail. A symbol is always in general and, however precise its translation, an artist can restore to it only its movement: there is no word-for-word rendering. Moreover, nothing is harder to understand than a symbolic work. A symbol always transcends the one who makes use of it and makes him say in reality more than he is aware of expressing. In this regard, the surest means of getting hold of it is not to provoke it, to begin the work without a preconceived attitude and not to look for its hidden currents. For Kafka in particular it is fair to agree to his rules, to approach the drama through its externals and the novel through its form.

The entire art of Franz Kafka lies in compelling the reader to reread. His ambiguous conclusions—or his deliberate refusal to provide endings at all—hint at explanations that are never stated directly, demanding that we revisit the narrative from an entirely different vantage point before any interpretation feels earned. At times his narratives sustain two contradictory readings at once, making a second encounter essential. This ambiguity was precisely what the author intended. Yet it would be an error to attempt a mechanical, point-by-point deciphering of every detail. A true symbol always operates in the realm of the general, and no matter how precise our commentary, an artist can only convey its dynamic movement: there can be no literal, one-to-one translation. Furthermore, few things are harder to comprehend than a symbolic work of art. A genuine symbol invariably surpasses the writer who deploys it, expressing far more than the author consciously intended. The most reliable way to approach it, therefore, is not to force a reading upon it, but to begin without preconceptions and refrain from hunting for hidden allegories. With Kafka especially, we must accept the terms he sets: entering the drama through its concrete surfaces and engaging the novel strictly through its external form.

The Philosophical Move

Aesthetics of the Open Symbol. Kafka deliberately constructs open-ended narratives that resist rigid, one-to-one allegorical decoding. True symbols transcend their authors' conscious intentions; they must be experienced through concrete narrative surfaces rather than forced into dogmatic systems.

There are works in which the event seems natural to the reader. But there are others (rarer, to be sure) in which the character considers natural what happens to him. By an odd but obvious paradox, the more extraordinary the character’s adventures are, the more noticeable will be the naturalness of the story: it is in proportion to the divergence we feel between the strangeness of a man’s life and the simplicity with which that man accepts it. It seems that this naturalness is Kafka’s. And, precisely, one is well aware what The Trial means. People have spoken of an image of the human condition. To be sure. Yet it is both simpler and more complex. I mean that the significance of the novel is more particular and more personal to Kafka. He learns this on the first pages of the novel he is pursuing in this world, and if he tries to cope with this, he nonetheless does so without surprise. He will never show sufficient astonishment at this lack of astonishment. It is by such contradictions that the first signs of the absurd work are recognized. The mind projects into the concrete its spiritual tragedy. And it can do so solely by means of a perpetual paradox which confers on colors the power to express the void and on daily gestures the strength to translate eternal ambitions.

One realizes quickly how difficult it is to discuss symbolism in a story whose most striking quality is its sheer naturalness. Yet naturalness is a deceptive and elusive category. There are narratives where bizarre events strike the reader as perfectly natural. There are others—far rarer—where the protagonist himself accepts whatever happens to him as entirely ordinary. Through a peculiar yet undeniable paradox, the more extraordinary the character's ordeals become, the more vivid that naturalness appears: it springs directly from the gulf between the bizarre absurdity of a man's fate and the unruffled simplicity with which he endures it. This very naturalness is the hallmark of Kafka's art. And that is why we immediately sense what The Trial conveys. Critics have called it an allegory for the universal human condition. Undoubtedly it is. Yet the truth is simultaneously simpler and far more intimate. By this I mean that the novel carries a significance intensely personal to Kafka himself. To a large extent, Kafka is speaking of his own plight, even as he lays bare our own private condition. He exists, and he is already condemned. He discovers this truth on the very first page of the life he pursues in this world, and while he attempts to navigate his sentence, he does so without the slightest shock. One can never marvel enough at this total absence of astonishment. It is through precisely such contradictions that we identify the signature of a genuinely absurd work of art. The intellect projects its internal spiritual tragedy into the tangible world. It accomplishes this through a continuous paradox: granting physical textures the power to evoke cosmic emptiness, and charging everyday habits with the weight of eternal yearnings.

The Philosophical Move

The Paradox of Unastonished Naturalness. Kafka's genius lies in characters who accept nightmarish existential condemnation without surprise. The Absurd arises from the friction between monstrous circumstances and the character's everyday composure.

One recognizes here the signature doctrine of existentialist philosophy: the teleological suspension of the ethical—truth standing in direct opposition to human morality. Camus's Core Philosophical Moves

1. The Absurd (L'Absurde)
Not "wackiness" or "goofiness." It is strictly relational: the violent collision between humanity's desperate hunger for meaning and the universe's total, stubborn silence. The Absurd exists in the collision itself.
2. Eluding / Evasion (L'Esquive)
Coping with the void through false grand narratives: religion, utopian political ideologies, or living strictly for "tomorrow." Camus calls hope the greatest evasion because it steals our only real possession: the present moment.
3. Philosophical Suicide
Forcing an artificial leap of faith (intellectual surrender) to make reality feel safe and explained again. Camus refuses this—he demands we keep our critical intellect 100% awake without numbing ourselves.
4. Lucidity (La Lucidité)
Staring directly into reality without illusions, without cosmic guarantees, and without flinching. Radical mental honesty.
5. Revolt (La Révolte)
Camus's ultimate conclusion: Knowing life has no cosmic meaning does not justify dying—it demands living with maximum defiance, creativity, and mortal intensity.
